headline: Cloud Attacks Bypass Your Detection Rules: Zero Lines for a Stolen IAM Key
summary: Traditional detection rules fail against cloud-native attacks. Learn how attackers exploit IAM API calls and what's needed to detect them.
details: Most security teams rely on detection rules built for traditional host and network environments. These rules often focus on process trees and endpoint activity, which are absent in cloud-native attacks.

Attackers can exploit stolen IAM credentials to perform reconnaissance and privilege escalation solely through API calls logged in CloudTrail. This bypasses traditional EDR and host-based detection methods.

Initial reconnaissance involves calls like sts:GetCallerIdentity and iam:List* to confirm credentials and enumerate account structure. While mundane on a host, this pattern from an unknown IP is highly suspicious in the cloud.

Privilege escalation often chains legitimate permissions, such as iam:PassRole with lambda:CreateFunction and lambda:InvokeFunction. This allows attackers to execute code with elevated privileges without using compromised credentials directly.

Detecting these cloud-native threats requires adapting detection engineering discipline to cloud logs. This means understanding normal API call patterns for identities and roles, and flagging unusual reconnaissance bursts.
The key is to write rules for specific, unusual combinations of IAM API calls that enable escalation, rather than just monitoring individual calls, many of which are normal for legitimate operations.
This approach is applicable across major cloud providers like AWS, Azure, and GCP, as well as Kubernetes, each having its own unique set of API calls and escalation paths.
Codelivly's Cloud Detection and Response Book aims to translate existing detection engineering skills into effective cloud log analysis, covering AWS, Azure, GCP, and Kubernetes.

headline_marked: Intel Xeon 7 [[Diamond Rapids]] CPU to Feature Up to 256 P-cores
headline: Intel Xeon 7 Diamond Rapids CPU to Feature Up to 256 P-cores
summary: Intel's next-gen server CPU, slated for 2027, will boast 1.28 GB of last-level cache and utilize the advanced 18A-P process node.
details: Intel has unveiled details about its upcoming Xeon 7 processors, codenamed Diamond Rapids, set to launch in data centers in 2027. These CPUs will feature up to 256 P-cores and a massive 1.28 GB of last-level cache, representing a significant leap in server processing power.

The Diamond Rapids CPUs will be built on Intel's enhanced 18A-P process node, which promises improved performance and lower power consumption compared to previous iterations. The architecture also introduces UCIe interconnects for chiplet communication and AVX 10.2 instructions for enhanced computational capabilities.

Intel is employing advanced packaging techniques, including Foveros Direct 3D and UCIe-S, to integrate multiple compute tiles (CBBs) and fabric hubs. Each CBB can house up to 16 P-cores, and the SoC design includes four base tiles and 16 core chiplets, all interconnected for efficient data flow.

A notable shift in design is the centralization of memory and I/O components, with cores pushed to the edges of the chip, a layout reminiscent of AMD's designs. This configuration aims to improve thermal management by reducing hot spots in the chip's center.

Memory support has also been enhanced, with Diamond Rapids featuring 16-channel DDR5 memory, supporting speeds up to 8,000 MT/s and up to 12,800 MT/s with MRDIMMs. This offers a substantial upgrade over the 12-channel support found in previous generations.

Connectivity options are robust, with support for 128 lanes of PCIe 6.0, CXL 3.0, and UPI 3, allowing for flexible configurations and high-speed data transfer. The I/O fabric also incorporates complexes for on-chip accelerators.
